query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys, the high configurational entropy promotes a nanoscale, uniform distribution of oxidation‐active elements (such as Cr, Al, or Ti) that selectively oxidize upon high‐temperature exposure to form a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale; concurrently, the inherent sluggish diffusion of the HEA matrix limits further oxide layer thickening or spallation, thereby retaining long‐term oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy synthesized with near‐equiatomic concentrations (or tailored ratios) of elements including one or more with high oxygen affinity (e.g., Cr, Al, or Ti) and exhibiting a largely single-phase solid solution with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Exposure of the HEA to high-temperature oxidizing conditions (e.g., static air) for extended durations.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures in the range of 800–900 °C under an ambient or controlled oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform nanoscale distribution of oxidation‐active elements and the intrinsically sluggish diffusion kinetics within the HEA matrix that restrict rapid elemental segregation and excessive oxide growth.
generation.mechanism: The selective oxidation of uniformly dispersed high oxygen-affinity elements forms a thin, continuous, and adherent oxide film that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress. Sluggish diffusion in the HEA retards the outward diffusion of alloying elements and the inward diffusion of oxygen, stabilizing the protective scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to alloys with non-uniform elemental distributions, the HEA will exhibit a lower oxidation rate (lower mass gain over time), develop a denser and more adherent oxide scale, and maintain this protective layer over longer exposures at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: A similar alloy system where oxidation-active elements are not uniformly distributed (e.g., showing segregation or secondary phases) that forms a less continuous or non-protective oxide scale under identical high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEAs that include sufficient concentrations of oxidation-active elements and are tested under oxidizing conditions at high temperatures (roughly 800–900 °C) in air; it may not apply if alternative oxidation pathways dominate or if the protective element content is insufficient.
generation.uncertainty: The precise relative contributions of uniform elemental distribution versus intrinsic sluggish diffusion to the observed oxidation resistance are not fully quantified, and other variables such as minor phase precipitations or surface roughness may also influence the protective scale formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with the same bulk chemistry: one set processed to achieve a highly uniform nanoscale distribution of oxidation-active elements (via controlled processing parameters) and a control set intentionally processed to promote elemental segregation. Subject both sets to static air oxidation at 850 °C for 100 hours.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to record mass gain as an indicator of oxidation rate.
Surface and cross-sectional characterization of the oxide scales via SEM, XRD, and TEM to assess continuity, phase composition, and adherence.
Adhesion testing of the oxide scale (e.g., scratch test) and microhardness measurements of the oxidized surface.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the uniform distribution do not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate (i.e., lower mass gain), or if they do not develop a more continuous, adherent, and protective oxide scale compared to the segregated control samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that a uniform elemental distribution combined with sluggish diffusion is responsible for the formation and retention of a protective oxide layer would be falsified.
